Assembly Lab

From a line of C to the bits in a register

Learn assembly by running instructions one at a time in your browser. The simulator supports a subset of 64-bit Arm instructions. In the lessons, you see C code beside its assembly instructions. After each instruction, you can inspect the register values and their bits, the flags and memory. You predict what will happen and write small assembly programs. Automatic checks test your answers and programs.

Start with
M0, L1: One addition
add w0, w0, w1
add w0, w0, w2
ret
w0
= 38
Next
Reset

Press Next to run one instruction. Watch the value and bits in register w0.

w0 holds 38.

Before you start

You need a little C, basic arithmetic and an understanding of binary numbers. You do not need any assembly experience.

Check what you need to know
The machine's state
Module 0
Fundamentals

Learn one operation at a time, follow a function call, then combine the instructions.

L1: One addition
L2: Adding a constant
L3: A tiny function
L4: Returning to the caller
L5: Subtraction and reuse
L6: Instructions in sequence
L7: Putting it together
Module 1
Registers and readings

Put values in registers and read one bit pattern as unsigned, signed or hexadecimal.

L1: Reading hexadecimal
L2: Signed and unsigned readings
L3: Arithmetic with four bits
L4: Arithmetic on register bits
L5: Loading a constant
L6: Building a constant
L7: Writing w and x registers
Module 2
Adding, subtracting and the flags

Add and subtract, follow the carries, and predict the four flags.

L1: Addition and its flags
L2: Flags and overflow
L3: Measuring elapsed ticks
L4: Subtraction flags and negation
Module 3
Logic, shifts and masks

Pick bits out of a word, and set, clear and move them.

L1: Changing one warning
L2: Reading and writing a field
L3: Choosing a shift
L4: Shifts and signed division
Choosing what runs next
Module 4
Compare and branch

Turn a C if statement into a compare and a branch, for signed and unsigned values.

L1: Choosing a signed or unsigned result
L2: Conditions and Boolean results
L3: Following a branch
L4: Zero and threshold branches
L5: Testing registers and bits
Module 5
Loops

Write counting loops, and find the loop that never ends.

L1: Following a loop
L2: Writing an upward loop
L3: Counting down with flags
L4: Testing before or after the body
L5: Stopping when useful work ends
Memory and wider values
Module 6
Loads, stores and widths

Move values of different sizes between memory and registers. See how a smaller value fills a larger register.

L1: Memory and addresses
L2: Choosing a transfer width
L3: Loading stored values
L4: Extending values in registers
Module 7
Arrays, strings and pointers

Walk through an array and a string by address.

L1: Selecting an array element
L2: Walking an array
L3: Strings and the zero byte
Module 8
Multiply and divide

Multiply into a result twice as wide, divide, and meet the cases that go wrong.

L1: Multiplication and addition
L2: Widening before multiplication
L3: Reading both halves of a product
L4: Division and remainders
L5: Calculating fuel consumption
L6: How GCC divides by a constant
Functions and C
Module 9
Calls and the stack

Call a function, return from it, and keep values safe on the stack.

L1: Saving a return address
L2: Preserving values across a call
L3: Following recursive calls
L4: Making recursive progress
Module 10
From C to assembly

Write C, watch it become instructions, and compare with a real compiler.

L1: Reading generated instructions
L2: Writing equivalent assembly
L3: Changing a C calculation
L4: Capping a result in C
L5: Reading a compiled loop
L6: Writing an equivalent loop
L7: Changing a loop boundary
L8: Writing repeated shifts in C
Module 11
Where C and the machine disagree

Explore what happens when a C program relies on behaviour that the language does not guarantee.

L1: C overflow and machine results
L2: Conversions and comparisons
L3: Checked addition
Module 12
Running ARM64 outside Assembly Lab

Assemble a bootable ARM64 program, trace its startup and debug it with GNU tools and QEMU.

L1: Building and booting an executable
L2: Loading the executable image
L3: Preparing the runtime state
L4: Connecting GDB and checking startup
L5: Stepping the native function
L6: Finding and repairing a native error
Module 13
Running on Raspberry Pi 5

Boot the assembly trip computer on a Raspberry Pi 5 and test it through its serial connector.

L1: Preparing and connecting the Pi
L2: Building and staging the Pi image
L3: Capturing the first Pi boot
L4: Breaking and restoring the Pi calculation
Optional, after the parts
Module A
The same programs on 32-bit ARM

Compare the course's A64 programs with recorded 32-bit Arm compiler output.

L1: A32 registers and returns
L2: A32 conditional moves and syntax
L3: A32 constant instructions
L4: A32 division helpers
Module B
L1: Two’s complement

Explore signed bit weights and fixed-width negation using four-bit patterns.

Module C
L1: C integer types and register widths

Optional reference: compare the widths and readings in three recorded C return values.

Module D
Floating-point values and instructions

Read floating-point bits, investigate rounding and compare recorded Arm arithmetic and conversions.

L1: Floating-point bits
L2: Rounding and precision
L3: Arm floating-point registers and arithmetic
L4: Converting values and copying bits
Where next?

Take a familiar function into your own project, or continue with native tools and a physical board.

Where next?

Digital Design builds a computer from gates. Bit Lab explores how computers represent and process data. Assembly Lab teaches Arm assembly through a browser simulator.

The machine's state

Fundamentals
